title: The 3 a.m. Notification That Gave Kavak Its First Sale
dek: In October 2016 a Venezuelan in Mexico launched a used-car site with about seven cars, some of them his team's own; days later, at 3 a.m., one sold.

story.founder: Carlos García Ottati, Loreanne García, Roger Laughlin
story.event: Launching a used-car platform in Mexico with a handful of cars and making the first sale
story.summary: In October 2016 Carlos García Ottati, a Venezuelan former Linio executive, launched Kavak in Mexico with his sister Loreanne García and Roger Laughlin to buy used cars from private owners, inspect and recondition them and resell them with a guarantee. By his account the first sale came at 3 a.m., days after the 2 October launch, from a catalogue of about seven cars. A first round of about 3 million dollars from Mountain Nazca followed, and in 2020 Kavak became Mexico's first start-up valued at over a billion dollars.
paragraphs: Early one morning in October 2016, Carlos García Ottati and his co-founder Roger Laughlin were still at work in García Ottati's home when a notification arrived: someone had bought a car from their phone. It was three in the morning, he later told Forbes, and it was Kavak's first sale, only days after the site went live on 2 October. The buyer, a student, had been browsing for about six days. The catalogue held roughly seven cars, some of them belonging to the team.

García Ottati, a Venezuelan with an Oxford MBA, had moved from Bogotá to Mexico City to run the marketplace at the online retailer Linio. The idea came from his own cars, though he has told the story differently over the years. Selling one in Colombia went badly, in one telling a scam and in another a six-month wait while a friend found a buyer, and a used car he bought in Mexico turned out to have problems. When he looked into the market, he said, he found that most used cars changed hands between private individuals, that fraud was common, and that in Mexico only about one sale in twenty was financed.

With his sister, Loreanne García, and Laughlin, and a team of no more than fifteen, he set out to buy cars from private owners, inspect and recondition them, and resell them with a guarantee. They started frugally; he later said that austerity at the beginning had been essential, because it made them build something sustainable from the first day. When they described the full plan to Héctor Sepúlveda of the fund Mountain Nazca, with reconditioning centres, an app and loans, García Ottati recalled that it sounded like science fiction. Sepúlveda backed them anyway, and the first round reached about 3 million dollars.

Kavak grew fast. In October 2020 it became the first Mexican start-up valued at more than a billion dollars, and in 2021 investors valued it at 8.7 billion. The pace brought strain. In late 2022, after a restructuring that cost dozens of jobs and a run of customer complaints about service, García Ottati took back direct charge of the Mexican business himself.

quote.text: Can a man be said, do you think, to know himself who knows his own name and nothing more? or must he not rather set to work precisely like the would-be purchaser of a horse
quote.locator: Book IV, chapter ii (section 25 in the usual numbering)
quote.source_title: The Memorabilia, tr. Henry Graham Dakyns, Project Gutenberg eBook #1177
quote.connection: Socrates goes on to say that a careful horse-buyer checks whether the animal is strong or weak, quick or slow, before trusting what he knows. Kavak was built on giving every car that kind of inspection. Socrates asks for the same honest inspection of ourselves.

reflection: Kavak's promise was an inspection that private car sales in Mexico rarely had: a proper look at the car, its papers and its engine before money changed hands. The idea came from García Ottati's own bad luck with cars, which he took seriously enough to study.

Socrates would have you turn that care inward. You probably check other things closely all day. It is rarer to ask, as plainly as a buyer would, what condition you are in this morning: what you can carry well at the moment, what is running low, and what you are asking yourself to do on a tank that needs filling.
invitation: Before you begin work today, give yourself a two-minute inspection: one thing in good order, one thing worn, and one load you will set down or share before the end of the week.

cross_checks.claim: Kavak was founded in Mexico in October 2016 by Carlos García Ottati, Loreanne García and Roger Laughlin
The idea came from García Ottati's own bad experiences selling and buying cars
Kavak's first funding round was about 3 million dollars from Mountain Nazca, led by Héctor Sepúlveda
In 2020 Kavak became the first Mexican start-up valued at over a billion dollars, and later reached 8.7 billion

research_notes: The founder's origin story varies between tellings, and the story says so. Forbes Perú (2021) and Revista Mercado (2022) say he was scammed when trying to sell his car; the 2022 Forbes interview (Spanish editions in Forbes Perú and Forbes Argentina) says a friend took six months to sell the car he left in Bogotá and that a used car he bought in Mexico had mechanical problems; El CEO (2026) says a bad experience buying a used car. A 2023 El Economista interview, seen only through a republication on a site not used here, adds that the money from his car sale vanished minutes after arriving and that police later told him a car he bought in Guadalajara was illegal. The story keeps only what the cited sources share: one car sale in Colombia that went badly and a used car in Mexico with problems. Founding date: Revista Mercado says he created Kavak in June 2016; Forbes and El CEO say October 2016, and García Ottati dates the platform's launch to 2 October 2016. The story uses October. The first-sale scene (3 a.m., his home, Laughlin present, a student buyer, about seven cars) rests on his own account in Forbes Perú (2021) and is attributed. Team size: 'no more than 15' (Forbes Perú 2021) and 'a team of 15' (Forbes 2022); the story says no more than fifteen. Financing statistic: Forbes Perú 2021 has him saying 5% of cars are financed in Latin America; Forbes 2022 has 5% of used-car sales financed in Mexico; the story uses the Mexico figure as 'about one sale in twenty'. Seed round: 3 million dollars from Mountain Nazca per Forbes Perú 2021 and Revista Mercado ('late 2016'); Forbes 2022 says Kaszek's Nicolás Berman backed the company from its first raise in December 2016. Founder quotations are in Spanish in the sources, so they are given as reported speech in English rather than as quotations. Later controversy: Bloomberg Línea (December 2022) reported lay-offs, customer complaints and García Ottati taking over the Mexican business; El CEO (2026) reported its own investigation into cars sold with irregular invoices, which Kavak's response in that article does not fully address. The story mentions the 2022 strain and does not make claims about the 2026 investigation. Valuation: 1.15 billion dollars in October 2020 and 8.7 billion after the 2021 rounds (Forbes; El CEO says eleven months after unicorn status). The Xenophon passage is Socrates questioning Euthydemus after the Delphic inscription 'Know thyself'; the excerpt ends mid-sentence before the horse-buyer's checks, which the connection paraphrases.
